lessons.title: The Core Agreement Rule
lessons.bite: The verb must match its subject in number, not the nearest noun. Singular subjects take the -s form of the verb; plural subjects don't. Get this one reflex right and you remove the most common agreement error in your writing.
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** Subject-verb agreement is checked on every single sentence you write, so one bad habit here costs marks over and over.

### The core rule
- In the present simple, a **singular subject** (he, she, it, one thing) takes the verb **+ s/es**: *the student works*.
- A **plural subject** takes the **base verb**, no -s: *the students work*.
- The -s is reversed between nouns and verbs: on a noun, -s means plural; on a verb, -s means singular. A correct sentence rarely has -s on both.

### The irregular pair to memorise
- **be:** is / was (singular) → are / were (plural)
- **have:** has (singular) → have (plural)

*The result is clear* vs *the results are clear*; *the number has risen* vs *the numbers have risen*.

lessons.title: Agreement's Eight Tricky Cases
lessons.bite: Most agreement errors don't come from the core rule -- they come from eight disguised cases where the real subject is hidden, delayed, or joined to another noun. Learn these eight and almost every agreement mistake in your essays disappears.
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** The core rule is easy; marks are lost on the cases where the true subject is hard to spot.

### The cases that decide your mark
- **Words between subject and verb:** ignore them -- the verb agrees with the true subject, not the nearest noun.
- **"The number of" (singular) vs "a number of" (plural):** *the number of tourists has increased*, but *a number of tourists were waiting*.
- **Collective nouns** (government, team, committee): singular in IELTS academic writing.
- **Indefinite pronouns** (each, everyone, neither) are always singular.
- **"Neither...nor", "either...or"**: the verb agrees with the nearer subject.
- **Compound subjects with "and"**: almost always plural.
- **"There is / there are"**: agrees with what comes after the verb.
- **Uncountable nouns and amounts** (information, ten years): singular, even though they look plural.

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Tense
lessons.bite: Of the twelve English tenses, only five do almost all the work in IELTS: present simple, present continuous, past simple, present perfect, and future forms. Master these five before worrying about the rest.
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** You can describe any graph and answer almost any Speaking question accurately with just five tenses.

### The five tenses that matter
- **Present simple** -- facts, habits, general truths, Task 2 positions.
- **Present continuous** -- what's happening now, current trends.
- **Past simple** -- finished events, historical graph data.
- **Present perfect** -- actions or trends that reach up to now.
- **Future forms** -- predictions and plans.

Two pairs inside this five cause almost all tense errors in Bangladeshi candidates' writing -- past simple vs present perfect, and present simple vs present continuous. Fixing those two pairs fixes most of your tense marks.

lessons.title: Tenses for Task 1 Trends
lessons.bite: Past simple or present perfect? It's the single most common tense confusion in Task 1 writing. The rule is about time: finished periods take past simple, periods reaching up to now take present perfect.
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** This is the single most common tense confusion for Bangladeshi candidates, and it's decisive in Task 1 trend description.

### The rule
- Use **past simple** when the time is finished and often stated: *in 2010, last year, two decades ago*.
- Use **present perfect** when the action reaches up to now, or the exact time doesn't matter: *since, for, over the past decade, recently*.

*The population rose in 2010* (a finished year) vs *the population has risen since 2010* (2010 up to the present).

### Spot the signal word
Time words like "in 2015" or "two decades ago" call for past simple; "since 2015", "for five years", or "so far" call for present perfect. Train yourself to scan the time expression first -- it tells you the tense before you even think about the verb.

lessons.title: Articles: A, An, The
lessons.bite: Every singular countable noun needs a deliberate choice: a/an, the, or no article at all. The rule turns on one question -- is this noun specific to both writer and reader, or not?
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** Article errors are some of the most frequent -- and most visible -- mistakes in Bangladeshi candidates' writing, because Bangla has no article system at all.

### The three articles (plus zero)
- **a/an** -- one, non-specific, singular, countable thing, usually the first mention. Choice depends on **sound, not spelling**: *a university* (consonant sound), *an hour* (silent h, vowel sound).
- **the** -- the noun is specific: already mentioned, unique (*the sun, the government*), or made specific by the words around it (*the number of cars*).
- **zero article** -- plurals and uncountables used in a general sense, and most proper nouns.

### The test to run
Ask: has this been mentioned before, or is there only one of it? If yes, use *the*. If it's one, unspecified example, use *a/an*. If neither applies, use no article at all.

lessons.title: Countable vs Uncountable Nouns
lessons.bite: Whether a/an is even an option depends on one distinction first: can this noun be counted? Uncountable nouns like information and advice never take a plural -s and never take a/an on their own.
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** This distinction decides whether article and plural rules even apply, so it has to come before everything else in Chapter 3.

### The two categories
- **Countable nouns** can be counted and have a plural form: *one book, two books*. They take *a/an* in the singular.
- **Uncountable nouns** are a single mass, with **no plural form** and **no a/an**: *information* (never *informations*), *water, advice*.

### The high-frequency IELTS set to memorise
*information, advice, knowledge, research, equipment, furniture, accommodation, traffic, progress, news, money, work, luggage, software, staff, homework*.

### To count the uncountable
Use a **partitive phrase**: not *an advice* but *a piece of advice*; not *a furniture* but *a piece of furniture* or *an item of furniture*.

lessons.title: Dependent Prepositions
lessons.bite: Many verbs, adjectives, and nouns are locked to a specific preposition with no logic behind the pairing -- you simply have to memorise each one as a fixed unit: depend ON, responsible FOR, an increase IN.
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** Dependent prepositions are pure memorisation, but they're everywhere in academic writing, and getting them wrong reads as a basic error even in an otherwise strong sentence.

### Learn them in blocks, by word type
- **Verb + preposition:** *depend on, lead to, result in, result from*.
- **Adjective + preposition:** *responsible for, interested in, aware of, capable of*.
- **Noun + preposition:** *an increase/rise in, a reason for, a solution to, an effect/impact on*.

There's no shortcut here -- memorise each pairing as a single chunk, not as two separate words, and practise them inside full sentences until the pairing feels automatic rather than looked-up.

lessons.title: Avoiding L1 Translation Traps
lessons.bite: A preposition shows a relationship -- place, time, or direction -- and its object follows it. When your English feels subtly wrong, check whether you've translated a Bangla preposition pattern directly instead of using the fixed English one.
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** Most preposition errors from Bangla speakers come from translating the L1 pattern word-for-word rather than learning the English pairing as its own fixed unit.

### What a preposition does
A preposition sits before a noun or pronoun and shows a relationship: *on the table* (place), *at three* (time), *into the room* (direction). The noun that follows is called its object.

### The habit to build
Whenever a preposition feels uncertain, resist translating from Bangla directly. Instead, recall the fixed English phrase as a whole chunk -- *depend on*, not "depend from" or "depend of" -- since English prepositions rarely map one-to-one onto their Bangla equivalents.

lessons.title: Building Complex Sentences
lessons.bite: Simple sentences get you to Band 5. Complex sentences -- one independent clause plus a dependent clause -- are what a Band 7 script controls and varies. Learn the two main tools: adverbial clauses and relative clauses.
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** Sentence variety is graded directly, and complex sentences are the single biggest lever for moving from Band 5-6 writing into Band 7+.

### The three sentence types
| Type | Structure | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Simple | one independent clause | *Cities offer jobs.* |
| Compound | two independent clauses + FANBOYS | *Cities offer jobs, but they are crowded.* |
| Complex | independent + dependent clause | *Although cities offer jobs, they are crowded.* |

A Band 5 script is mostly simple sentences. A Band 6 script mixes simple and compound. A **Band 7 script controls complex sentences and varies them** -- using both adverbial clauses (if/although/because) and relative clauses (who/which/that).

lessons.title: Punctuating Relative Clauses
lessons.bite: Defining and non-defining relative clauses look almost identical -- the only difference is a pair of commas, but that punctuation changes the meaning of the sentence entirely.
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** This is the part of relative clauses that actually carries marks -- the commas aren't decorative, they change what the sentence means.

### The two types
- A **defining clause** identifies *which one* and is essential -- no commas: *Students who cheat are expelled* (only the cheating ones).
- A **non-defining clause** adds extra, non-essential information, fenced with commas on both sides: *The students, who were tired, left early* (all of them).

### Two rules that follow
- Use **that** only in defining clauses. In non-defining clauses, use **which** or **who** -- never *that*.
- Don't repeat the subject with a pronoun after the relative clause (a very common Bangla-influenced error).

### A Band 8 touch
Reduced relative clauses tighten the sentence further: *governments that invest in renewables* → *governments investing in renewables*.

lessons.title: Active to Passive Transformation
lessons.bite: Whatever the tense, the passive always ends in the past participle -- only the 'be' form in front of it changes to carry the time. Learn that one pattern and you can transform any active sentence.
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** The passive appears across every tense, and IELTS Task 1 and academic writing lean on it constantly -- so the transformation needs to be automatic.

### The pattern
The tense lives in the **be** part; the past participle stays the same.

- Present simple: *Workers transport the goods.* → *The goods are transported.*
- Present continuous: *Workers are transporting the goods.* → *The goods are being transported.*
- Past simple: *Workers transported the goods.* → *The goods were transported.*

Notice the constant: whatever the tense, you always end with the past participle (*transported*), and only the *be* form in front of it changes to carry the time.

lessons.title: Passive Voice for Process Writing
lessons.bite: The passive isn't a default -- it's a tool for three specific situations: when the doer is unknown or obvious, when you want an objective tone, and when you're describing a process. Process diagrams are exactly that third case.
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** Process-diagram Task 1s are almost impossible to write naturally without the passive, since the steps matter more than who performs them.

### When to choose the passive
- The **doer is unknown, obvious, or unimportant**: *New traffic laws were introduced in 2019* (who introduced them is obvious).
- You want an **objective, impersonal tone**: *It is widely believed that education reduces poverty* (more academic than "many people believe").
- You are **describing a process** -- a sequence of steps where the focus is the material or product moving through stages, not the people carrying them out.

For process diagrams specifically, keep every step in the passive and in a consistent tense (usually present simple) so the sequence reads as a system, not a story about workers.

lessons.title: Conditional Sentence Forms
lessons.bite: The four conditionals sit on a scale of reality, from always-true to no-longer-possible. Choosing the right one is choosing how real you want your claim to sound -- get this wrong and a genuine possibility reads as pure fantasy, or vice versa.
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** Conditional choice signals how confident you are in a claim, which matters enormously in Task 2 argumentation.

### The four conditionals, as a scale of reality
- **Zero** -- general truth / scientific fact: *If you heat ice, it melts.*
- **First** -- a real, likely future possibility: *If taxes rise, consumption will fall.*
- **Second** -- imagined or unlikely: hypothetical present/future.
- **Third** -- impossible now, because the moment has passed.

Read the scale in order: zero is always true, first is realistically possible, second is imagined, third is impossible.

### A formal note
Formal English uses **were** for all subjects in the second conditional -- *If the government were to act...* -- and this is the safer choice in Writing.

lessons.title: Hedging for Academic Tone
lessons.bite: Band 5 writing is full of absolutes -- always, never, everyone. Band 8 writing hedges its claims with modals and tendency verbs, which paradoxically makes them sound more credible, not less confident.
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** Hedging is one of the fastest, most learnable upgrades from Band 6-7 writing into Band 8 writing -- it's a toolkit, not a talent.

### What hedging means
Hedging softens a claim so it isn't an absolute statement. *"Immigration boosts the economy"* is a claim you can't fully prove; *"Immigration can boost the economy"* is one you can defend.

### The hedging toolkit
- **Modal verbs of possibility:** may, might, could, can.
- **Verbs of tendency:** tend to, be likely to, appear to, seem to.
- **Adverbs of frequency/degree:** often, generally, in many cases, to some extent, relatively.
- **Impersonal frames:** it is often argued that, it could be said that.

Hedging is not weakness or vagueness -- it's precision about how certain you actually are.

lessons.title: Inversion for Emphasis
lessons.bite: Inversion fires when a negative or limiting adverbial moves to the front of the sentence -- never, rarely, not only. Learn this trigger set as a fixed list and the auxiliary-before-subject pattern becomes automatic.
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** Correct inversion is one of the clearest Band 9 signals an examiner looks for -- and one of the easiest to get wrong if attempted carelessly.

### The trigger expressions
Inversion is triggered when one of these negative or limiting adverbials moves to the front:
- **Never / Never before** -- *Never before has the country faced such a crisis.*
- **Rarely / Seldom** -- *Rarely do politicians admit their mistakes.*
- **Not only... (but also)** -- *Not only does it cut costs, but it also saves time.*

### The mechanism
Memorise the trigger set first. Once the trigger is at the front, the subject and auxiliary verb swap places exactly as they do in a question -- that's the whole mechanism.

lessons.title: Cleft Sentences
lessons.bite: A cleft sentence splits one idea into two clauses to spotlight a single element. It's gentler than inversion and far more natural in both Writing and Speaking -- two patterns cover almost every use.
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** Cleft sentences are a natural, low-risk way to add emphasis without the stricter grammar rules that inversion demands.

### It-cleft
Structure: **It + is/was + the emphasised element + that/who + the rest.**
Plain: *The lack of funding caused the failure.* → Cleft: *It was the lack of funding that caused the failure.* (spotlight on the cause)

### What-cleft (pseudo-cleft)
Structure: **What + clause + is/was + the emphasised element.**
Plain: *We need better public transport.* → Cleft: *What we need is better public transport.* (spotlight on the solution)

The what-cleft is especially useful for opening a point emphatically: *What many governments overlook is the long-term cost of inaction.*

lessons.title: Nominalisation for Academic Density
lessons.bite: Nominalisation turns a verb or adjective into a noun -- decide becomes decision, difficult becomes difficulty. Once an idea is a noun it can become the subject of a sentence, which is exactly what gives academic prose its abstract, concept-driven feel.
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** Nominalisation is the single grammatical habit most responsible for the difference between conversational English and academic English.

### The core transformation
Nominalisation converts an action word (verb) or a quality word (adjective) into a thing word (noun). Once an idea is a noun, it can become the **subject** of a sentence.

### Common families to build from
| Verb | Noun | Adjective | Noun |
|---|---|---|---|
| decide | decision | difficult | difficulty |
| reduce | reduction | able | ability |
| analyse | analysis | poor | poverty |
| grow | growth | important | importance |

Practising these families in both directions -- spotting the verb form and producing the noun form on demand -- is what makes nominalisation available under exam pressure rather than something you only recognise when reading.

lessons.title: The Self-Editing Checklist
lessons.bite: Trying to catch every grammar error in one read is how mistakes slip through. Run a separate, single-focus pass for each rule -- agreement, then tense, then articles, then prepositions -- because specialists beat generalists when proofreading.
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** This is the checklist that ties every earlier chapter together into a single, repeatable editing routine you can run on any essay before you submit it.

### The self-editing checklist, in order
1. **Agreement pass** -- check every verb against its true subject (Chapter 1).
2. **Tense pass** -- check that every time frame is correct and consistent (Chapter 2).
3. **Article pass** -- check every singular noun for a/an/the/zero (Chapter 3).
4. **Preposition pass** -- check dependent and data prepositions (Chapter 4).

Do a **separate pass for each item** rather than trying to catch everything in one read-through. Specialists beat generalists when proofreading -- a single-focus pass catches errors a general read-through misses entirely.

lessons.title: Polishing Speaking Transcripts
lessons.bite: Speaking is graded on the same Grammatical Range and Accuracy criterion as Writing, but the target is different: controlled flexibility in real time, not written density. Fix base accuracy first, then add one complex sentence and one tense contrast.
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** Candidates often over-prepare Writing grammar and under-prepare the same criterion for Speaking, where the goal is different.

### The upgrade toolkit for Speaking, in order of value
1. **Fix base accuracy first** -- agreement, tense, and articles, since these cost the most.
2. **Add one complex sentence** -- a because, although, or which clause to connect two ideas.
3. **Add a tense contrast** -- move between past, present, and future to show range: *I used to..., but now I...*

### The goal
Accurate, flexible spoken English -- not a memorised paragraph. One natural complex sentence and one tense contrast in a Part 2 answer will do more for your score than a rehearsed idiom.
